title: DfE Decoded #159: SEND Training Is Becoming Everyone's Business
author: Paul Urry
summary: Paul Urry reviews the new national SEND and inclusion training for mainstream schools and argues its main message is that inclusive teaching, not specialist referral, is the starting point. He notes the training targets teachers and teaching assistants rather than SENDCos, and that it begins with familiar craft such as clear explanation, explicit instruction, scaffolding, feedback and calm routines. He warns that more support is not automatically better, since scaffolds that never fade, reduced tasks and permanent adult support can create dependency and lower expectations. He favours planning from one ambitious learning intention and adapting the route, and he welcomes the shift from fixed diagnostic labels to five Areas of Development, starting with speech, language and communication. Using working memory and instruction-following as examples, he shows how apparent behaviour problems can be language problems. He ends with advice that leaders should select training to fit their school's needs and should not treat inclusive teaching as a cheap substitute for specialist support.
points: Urry argues that SEND is being repositioned as every teacher's responsibility, with the universal offer of strong classroom teaching as the foundation.
He challenges the assumption that more adult support and extra provision is better, since scaffolds, reduced tasks and one-to-one adults can limit independence and thinking.
He contrasts planning different objectives for groups in advance with planning one ambitious intention and adapting the route, which keeps the destination high.
Using a five-step classroom instruction as an example, he shows how working memory limits can look like poor behaviour, and recommends fewer steps, pauses, visuals and checking understanding.
He cautions that label-driven strategy sheets should give way to understanding the barrier first, and that inclusive teaching must not replace specialist support where it is needed.
quotes: SEND is increasingly being positioned as everybody’s responsibility, with inclusive teaching as the starting point.

A strong universal offer doesn’t mean identical provision for everybody. It means getting everyday classroom teaching as strong and inclusive as possible, while recognising that some children will still need something more.
A scaffold that never disappears can create dependency. A reduced task can reduce thinking. An adult permanently sitting beside a child can unintentionally limit independence.

The first approach risks deciding what children are capable of before the lesson has even started. The second keeps expectations high but recognises that some children may need a different route to get there.
Before deciding that a child won’t do something, it is worth making sure they understood what they were being asked to do.
The danger is that the label starts driving the provision rather than the pupil. The better approach is to understand the barrier first.
Inclusive teaching should mean children get the right support sooner. It shouldn’t become a cheaper substitute for specialist support where specialist support is genuinely needed.
That doesn’t make every teacher a SEND specialist. It makes inclusive teaching part of being a teacher.
